I've attached a brief usage report and a matrix that maps the squads to subaccounts. Happy to hop on a quick call.

Thanks,

Jordan / team — quick findings from logs:
- Two Org IDs are distinct and both have corporate emails tied to echolabs.ai. No immediate evidence of scripted account creation.
- However, Squad A and Squad B activity both originate from the same set of corporate CIDR ranges and the same handful of public IPs (likely VPN/proxy used by their infra team). That's not inherently fraud but increases risk for chained requests.
- Past extension in Feb was small; token consumption there was consistent with E2E tests.
- No open fraud alerts in the last 6 months, but I recommend gating: 1) limit any promo to a short expiry (7 days), 2) require usage tagging and automated quotas per Org ID, and 3) collect a formal sign-off from EchoLabs security to attest the isolated test environments.

If legal/commercial still think 150k is too high, we can propose 75k with the gating above.

—Soojin
Security & Trust, Redwood Inference

Thanks, Soojin — that read is helpful. My take:
- We should not make a broad policy exception for chained extensions. Pattern matches our fraud vectors (same org, proxy IPs).
- Offer a controlled compromise: 75k promo tokens total split across the two Org IDs (37.5k each), 7-day expiry, usage tags + quota enforced, and require EchoLabs security sign-off on isolation. If they decline, offer a discounted 30-day dedicated trial (50% off first month) with a narrower SLA.

Jordan — can you communicate the offer to Alex and get the security attestation? Include legal if they accept so we can record the exception and tags.

Marissa
Head of Sales, Redwood Inference
